text: Class Notes: JAMM 448, FOIA 11/6/18 9:30-10:45, TLC 249 Slide Two: Class Reminders They are turning in a libel homework exercise. I will not have them graded for the test, but I will have an answer rubric on BB Learn by Wednesday. I will email about availability for extended office hours on Wednesday, 11/7 for Test Review, paper questions, etc. Slide Three: FOI Presumption is disclosure- unless is it exempted, we should know what federal agencies are doing- THEY HAVE NOTHING TO HIDE Freedom of information impacts our roles as citizens, and the role of the people who govern us How do we handle transparency in an age of big data? How do we handle information leaks that fall outside of FOIA? How do we handle domestic surveillance of US citizens? How do we handle tools like social media being utilized for terror? Slide Four: Freedom of Information Federal law that applies to records of executive agencies Ask them for examples of executive agencies (FCC, FDA, FAA, FTC, etc.) Who FOIA doesn’t apply to (other laws capture most of these records) Gvt. in the Sunshine is the corollary law for agency meetings Slide Five: What is a Record? Anything that is part of the governing record (paper, email, etc.) For it to be a “record” under FOIA, and available for the public to request, the agency must have control of the record Loophole- agencies divest themselves of records Slide Six: Hillary Clinton’s Emails Hillary Clinton was Secretary of State- used personal email address (and server) to conduct state business Those emails no longer “official government record” because the agency she worked for didn’t have control of them Contravenes spirit of FOIA Slide Seven: Widespread Patterns 2015 survey of over 400 federal employees 33% use personal email sometimes 1/3 of the records that should be available under FOIA are not Slide Eight: Widespread Patterns 27% respondents cited FOIA as something that hinders internal office email What do we think about that? Slide Nine: Who Can Make a Request Few guidelines on requesting records Pretty much anyone (but a hostile foreign government, ie: North Korea) Must be able to reasonable describe record- more specific the better (emails dealing with water quality for Coulee Dam Dec. 1-Dec. 30 vs. emails dealing with water quality) Slide 10: Mechanics of Request Generally 20 business days to respond Should either say “here are the records” OR cite one of the nine exemptions BUT… Slide 11: Another Loophole Some agencies just ignore problematic requests, let them sit unanswered completely Department of Defense 2015- Air Force vs. DCAA No strong enforcement mechanism- complain to agencies about agencies not complying… courts often side with agencies Slide 12: FOIA Enforcement Presidential administrations have a lot of sway in how well FOIA is enforced Beginning of administration- send out “FOIA memo” telling agencies how thoroughly they should comply with record requests… Slide 13: Mechanics of FOIA Requests Revisited Just highlighting this visually Slide 14: Presidents and the FOIA Tell them NOT to write this slide down- examples, not things I will test them on Varying presidential attitudes on government transparency/FOIA Explore/discuss a bit Slide 15: Exemptions Certain categories of information can be withheld Aside from Exemption 1 (National Security) agencies CAN cite exemptions, but can also release records that would fall under exemptions When presidents urge opacity, agencies withhold more records because they can, not because they have to Slide 16-22: Exemptions 1-7 Review briefly, do they have questions? Slide 23: Financial Records Why protect banks? Timing of FOIA (began talks in 1940s, only 20 years after Great Depression, passed in 1966… what happened with bank runs and the Great Depression? People panicked and withdrew large amounts of cash, banks ran out of cash on hand, cause more panic) Gvt. Decided to regulate banks and not give the public information (trust in the banking institutes… how has that gone?) Slide 24: Exemption 9 Why protect oil and gas? Why not other industries? Why are they special? Lyndon B Johnson was president when FOIA was passed- where was he from? Required Exemption 9 to appease main contributors- oil and gas lobby Example of how lobbying can and does have direct impact on our laws Slide 25: Government in the Sunshine -amendment to include meetings - same exemptions plus a tenth one Slide 26: State Laws Don’t need to know details from the books, focus on federal (model off of federal) Slides 27-31: Challenges to Access: Privatization- if private companies are doing gvt. work the records aren’t open to FOIA Technology- so much data, easy to “delete” records “accidentally” (ie: George W. Bush administration… most of the emails should have been made available under Presidential Records Act eventually) Leaking data- leaks from Ellsberg (Pentagon Papers- they will know this case), Snowden, Manning, all examples of information we would NOT have gotten otherwise (exempt under Exemption 1: National Security)- should we have information like this? Domestic surveillance- post 9/11 operating with Mosaic Theory- difficult to see movement of lone wolfs or terror cells, get ALL the information, been conducting warrantless surveillance of US citizens, which is illegal… since it falls under Exemption 1, we don’t really have much information or a say (one of the things we learned from the Snowden leak)
